title: The Clay Jar Translation™ (CJT)
summary: A new English Bible, translated afresh from the oldest available witnesses and given freely to the public domain. This is the project home: the charter, the prayer, the sources, the canon tracker, and the translated text, beginning with the complete book of Genesis.

items.label: Copyright
items.value: None. Dedicated to the public domain

items.label: Scope
items.value: Old Testament, Apocrypha, New Testament, Pseudepigrapha

items.label: Translators
items.value: Jose Santiago, with AI assistance; open to scholarly review

blocks.text: The Dead Sea Scrolls, the oldest Bible manuscripts we have, survived for two thousand years because someone sealed them in clay jars in the caves near Qumran. The prophet Jeremiah was told to put his deeds in a clay jar “so that they may last for many days” (Jeremiah 32:14). The apostle Paul wrote that “we have this treasure in clay jars, so that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us” (2 Corinthians 4:7). And in Genesis 2:7 God forms the first human from the ground like a potter shaping clay.
The name says what we hope this work will be: a plain, humble container that carries the oldest words faithfully to readers for many years, where the treasure is the word and not the jar.
The Clay Jar Translation, including its text, footnotes, introductions, and tables, is given to the public domain. No one owns it, and no one ever may.

We, the makers of this translation, give up every copyright and related right we might hold in this work, everywhere in the world, as fully as the law allows. Where the law does not allow such a waiver, we grant everyone a permanent, free, unconditional permission to use the work in any way.

You may copy it, print it, read it aloud, record it, quote any amount of it, put it on a website or in an app, translate it into other languages, revise it, sell it, or give it away, all without asking anyone and without paying anyone. Credit is welcome but not required.

The text itself is public domain. The name “Clay Jar Translation” and the CJT logo are trademarks of Jose Santiago. This protects only the name, not the words. If you copy the text without changing it, you may call it the Clay Jar Translation or the CJT. If you change the wording, you are free to do so, but please give your version a different name and do not use the CJT name or logo on it. That way readers can always tell the original from a changed version.
The word of God was given freely, and we give this translation freely in return.

Holy God, Maker of heaven and earth, you spoke and light came into being, and you formed us from the dust and breathed your life into us. We come to you now as clay in the hands of the potter. We ask you to guide this work of translation. Open our eyes to see what your word truly says, and give us humility to set aside what we wish it said. Where the old manuscripts speak with one voice, help us to carry their words faithfully; where they differ, give us patience, honesty, and wisdom to weigh them well.

Guard us from pride, from carelessness, and from adding to or taking away from your words. Send your Spirit, who first moved over the waters, to move over our minds and our hands as we work. Let every page we make be clear, true, and free, so that people who have never held a Bible, and people who have read it all their lives, may find you in it. Bless Jose and everyone who will read, check, correct, and share this translation. We offer it back to you, for it was always yours. In your holy name we pray. Amen.

steps.title: Word for word by default
steps.detail: We follow the Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek closely (formal equivalence), keeping word order, repeated words, and images wherever English can carry them.

steps.title: Thought for thought only where needed
steps.detail: Where a literal rendering would mislead or be unclear in English (idioms, wordplay, doubled nouns), we translate the meaning (dynamic equivalence) and always give the literal wording in a footnote marked “Thought for thought. Literally…”.

steps.title: Plain, lasting English
steps.detail: We use standard English that has been stable for generations and should stay clear for at least 20 more years: no slang, no trendy idioms, no thee, thou, or -eth endings, and no words that are changing meaning quickly.

steps.title: Consistent key words
steps.detail: Important terms keep the same English wherever possible (for example, nefesh chayyah is always “living being” or “living creature”), so readers can trace them through the Bible.

steps.title: Show the evidence
steps.detail: When ancient witnesses differ in a way that changes meaning, we say so in a footnote and name the witnesses.

rows: The personal name of God, YHWH, printed wherever the Hebrew has it. Older English Bibles print it “the LORD.” See the note on Genesis 2:4.

Hebrew elohim or el used of the true God; Greek theos. Elohim is a title, not a personal name.
Names such as El Shaddai and El Elyon are transliterated, with the meaning in a footnote where each first appears. See the table below.

Every person named in the Hebrew is named in the text, with the meaning of significant names in a footnote at first use (marked uncertain where it is). Hebrew ha-adam, “the human,” is rendered “Adam” from 2:7 where the one man is meant; “humankind” where it means the human race (1:26–27; 5:2). The woman is named Eve from 3:20.

blocks.text: Ancient standards varied by place and period (a longer “royal” cubit of about 20.5 inches, or 52 cm, was also used), so all conversions are approximate.

We start from the oldest surviving witnesses and work forward. A printed base text gives us a stable verse-by-verse starting point; older manuscripts then correct it where the evidence is strong. We work only from public-domain editions, manuscript images, and the factual readings of manuscripts. We never copy wording from any copyrighted English translation, such as the NIV, ESV, NRSV, NASB, CSB, NLT, NKJV, or NET.

steps.title: Watch
steps.detail: We follow new finds and new readings, such as the Greek Minor Prophets fragments recovered from the Judean Desert in 2021, and texts recovered by multispectral imaging of palimpsests.

steps.title: Wait for publication
steps.detail: We use a new manuscript once its readings are published and its age and authenticity are confirmed; we never rely on unverified or unprovenanced items.

steps.title: Weigh
steps.detail: Age matters, but so do the quality of the copy and agreement with other witnesses. An older reading is adopted when it best explains how the others arose.

steps.title: Revise and record
steps.detail: Changes go into the next numbered edition, with a footnote naming the new witness, so every edition stays traceable.

blocks.text: Status as of 23 October 2026: Genesis is complete (chapters 1 to 50); every other book is planned. Books are grouped by tradition, not by authority. The Apocrypha are accepted as Scripture by Catholic and Orthodox churches; the Pseudepigrapha are included for study and for their place in ancient Jewish and Christian life. 1 Enoch and Jubilees are part of the Ethiopian Orthodox canon.

sections.heading: An honest note on this draft

blocks.text: This translation was drafted by Jose Santiago working with an AI assistant. It has not yet been reviewed by Hebrew, Aramaic, or Greek scholars. Corrections are welcome, and every reviewed passage will be marked as such in later editions.

Translation is a human and spiritual task as well as a technical one. Please read this draft alongside other translations, test it against the original languages where you can, and share what you find, so that each edition becomes more faithful than the last.
